title: Microgravity burner-generated spherical diffusion flames: experiment and computation
summary: Pre-flight work of the PI group (Law, Princeton); 2.2 s drop-tower tests of H2/CH4/inert flames on a 1.27 cm bronze porous sphere, with transient detailed-chemistry simulation. Steady state could not be reached in 2.2 s; radiative reabsorption was needed to predict extinction time; visible luminosity did not track flame strength. It predates the 2019-2020 s-Flame ISS runs and contains no s-Flame data.

items.claim: Drop-tower precursor, not ISS s-Flame data.
items.quote: Microgravity experiments were conducted in the 2.2-s drop-tower facility at the NASA Glenn Research Center

items.claim: Steady spherical diffusion flames cannot be reached in a 2.2 s drop tower, which is why orbit was needed.
items.quote: although steady-state behavior should exist for such flames, the experimental and computational results indicated that it cannot be reached within the 2.2-s microgravity duration for the fuels and mass-flow rates tested

items.claim: Visible luminosity is not a reliable measure of flame strength.
items.quote: the lack of correspondence between the visible flame luminosity and flame strength, as related to flame temperature and heat release rate, was noted

It predates the 2019-2020 s-Flame ISS runs and contains no s-Flame data.

items.claim: Low-pressure normal-gravity precursor, not ISS data.
items.quote: An inverse flame configuration was employed with the oxidizer being ejected from a porous sphere burner into a fuel (H 2 ) environment in a low-pressure (0.096 atm) chamber to effectively minimize buoyancy.

items.claim: Oscillation preceding radiative extinction is the behaviour the record says theory predicted and s-Flame looked for.
items.quote: However at the radiation-induced limit extinction is preceded by oscillations in the flame luminosity that grows in amplitude before extinction.
